analysis.one_liner: Shields oil, gas, and coal companies from climate change lawsuits and voids state laws making them pay for climate damages.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 23 Republican cosponsors, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote since April 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to file any lawsuit against oil, gas, and coal companies seeking money or other relief for harm caused by climate change — including claims that the companies misled the public about their products. It would also wipe out every state law that makes energy companies pay into funds for climate-related damage (so-called "climate superfund" laws), declare federal law the only authority over climate change, and force courts to immediately throw out all climate lawsuits already in progress.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and coal companies, and the trade associations that represent them. Dozens of states, cities, and counties have sued major energy companies, seeking billions of dollars to cover costs of floods, wildfires, hurricanes, and sea-level rise, arguing the companies knew their products drove climate change and concealed it. This bill would end all of those cases and bar new ones, removing the industry's single largest legal and financial exposure.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans any "climate suit" — any claim for damages, punitive damages, injunctions, or restitution against an energy company for past or future harm from climate change — from being filed or kept alive in any federal or state court [S2].

It defines "energy" broadly to cover crude oil, natural gas, refined petroleum products, and coal, and covers anyone in the business of mining, producing, refining, transporting, distributing, manufacturing, or selling those fuels [S2].

It voids every state "energy penalty law" — laws that require energy companies to compensate for climate-related costs, including state climate superfund laws — declaring them "void and of no effect" [S2].
It would immediately dismiss every climate lawsuit already pending on the date of enactment, wiping out years of litigation by states and municipalities at a stroke [S2].

The ban covers claims based on marketing, alleged misrepresentation, or alleged failure to warn — meaning even fraud-style claims that companies deceived the public about climate science could not proceed [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State and local taxpayers, and people who suffer climate-related losses. Costs that courts or state superfund laws might have assigned to energy companies — flood defenses, wildfire recovery, storm damage — would stay with the public instead. The bill also overrides the decisions of state legislatures that chose to make polluters pay for climate adaptation.

drawbacks.text: The bill declares that attributing local floods, droughts, hurricanes, wildfires, or heat waves to energy companies "lack[s] scientific credibility," a premise many climate scientists and the pending lawsuits dispute [S2].

It overrides state legislatures and courts wholesale: state laws passed democratically are voided, and even lawsuits already pending are dismissed, raising serious federalism questions about Congress wiping out state law and state courts' jurisdiction [S2].

By barring claims based on "alleged misrepresentation" or "any other speech," it would shield companies even from claims that they knowingly lied about their products' harms — a protection no other consumer-facing industry enjoys [S2].

Defenders argue the lawsuits target conduct that was lawful when it happened and that climate policy should be set by Congress and federal agencies, not by scattered state courts and juries imposing retroactive liability nationwide [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit flows almost entirely to a handful of large energy companies facing tens of billions of dollars in potential liability. The cost falls on the public: money states hoped to recover from energy companies for climate adaptation would come from taxpayers instead, and people harmed by climate-driven disasters would lose the courtroom as a remedy. The bill's legal theory (that federal law exclusively occupies the field) is contested, and its breadth — covering even fraud claims — goes beyond what is needed to stop what its sponsor calls excessive litigation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not held a hearing or voted on it, so nothing has changed yet for the lawsuits it targets.

narrative.text: Rep. Harriet Hageman introduced the bill on April 16, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1].
No further action — no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral [S4].
The bill has 23 cosponsors, all Republicans, out of 223 House Republicans [S3].
While the bill sits in committee, state climate superfund laws remain in effect and climate lawsuits against energy companies continue in the courts [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, oil, gas, and coal companies facing climate litigation are better off: the bill has gone nowhere, which means the state laws and pending lawsuits seeking money from them remain intact. States and local governments pursuing those claims have also gained time, though the bill could be revived before the Congress ends.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies facing climate suits

for.name: Reps. Paul Gosar, Dan Crenshaw, Pete Stauber, and Barry Moore
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on; the bill has drawn no recorded opposition either, because it has not advanced to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would wipe out pending climate lawsuits against them and bar new ones, including claims that they misled the public about their products. Money states hoped to recover for flood, wildfire, and storm costs would stay with the companies and come from taxpayers instead.
Coal is explicitly covered by the bill's definition of "energy," so coal producers would be shielded from the same climate liability claims.

industries.industry: State governments with climate superfund laws
industries.note: The bill voids state laws that require energy companies to pay into climate adaptation funds, taking away a revenue source states chose for themselves and shifting those costs back to their taxpayers.
Trade associations are named in the bill's definitions, suggesting they face related claims; the blanket ban on climate suits would protect them too.

analysis.trajectory: With only 23 cosponsors and no committee action nearly a year into the two-year Congress, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or floor vote and will probably die in the Judiciary Committee when this Congress ends, as most bills referred to committee do.
